speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The period of incarceration is an opportunity to rehabilitate offenders, to minimise the possibility of re-offending after release.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In my visits to the prisons and engagements with inmates and ex-offenders, I have come to see that rehabilitation, with strong community and family support, can be an effective means to prevent re-offending.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: SPS rehabilitates and prepares inmates for reintegration into society by providing programmes in prison to address their re-offending risks and needs, and equip them with relevant knowledge and skills.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: These programmes include psychology-based correctional programmes, family programmes, work programmes, skills training and religious programmes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: As Members may know, rehabilitation in prison alone is not enough.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Research has shown that inmates will have better rehabilitation outcomes when rehabilitation in prison is complemented by community-based programmes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: These programmes allow inmates to be closely supervised and supported while they apply the skills that they had learnt in prison.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Over the years, SPS has expanded community corrections.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In 1985, the Prisons Act was amended to introduce the Work Release Scheme, or WRS.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: WRS allows inmates to work outside prison, under supervision, at the tail-end of their imprisonment sentence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In 2000, the Prisons Act was amended to provide for the Home Detention Scheme or HDS, which allows eligible inmates to serve the tail-end of their imprisonment sentence outside prison, such as at their residence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The intent is to facilitate their reintegration into society under strict conditions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Prisons Act was amended in 2014 to introduce the Mandatory Aftercare Scheme, or MAS.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The MAS provides enhanced community support, counselling and case management, with tight supervision, to released inmates who are at a higher risk of re-offending or need more reintegration support.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: While on this scheme, supervisees need to comply with conditions such as curfew hours and electronic monitoring.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: There have also been shifts in the drug rehabilitation regime.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In 2019, a more calibrated approach was introduced for drug abusers to distinguish between abusers who have only consumed drugs and those who have concurrently committed other criminal offences.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Prior to this policy change, drug abusers arrested for the third time onwards would be sentenced to imprisonment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Since 2019, such abusers who do not face any other concurrent criminal charge will instead undergo rehabilitation in the Drug Rehabilitation Centre, or DRC, run by SPS.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: As part of the DRC regime, suitable abusers can progress to be placed on community-based programmes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The improvement in recidivism bears testimony to our rehabilitation and reintegration efforts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: These results give us the confidence to introduce an improved work rehabilitation scheme, called the Employment Preparation Scheme, or EmPS, to enhance inmates' employability and reintegration.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The WRS only allows inmates to be released for work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Under the existing law, inmates on the WRS are unable to participate in educational or training activities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The new EmPS will allow inmates to undergo skills training and education in the community.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The EmPS will complement the work programmes and skills training provided by SPS and Yellow Ribbon Singapore (YRSG) in prison.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: To provide for the EmPS, clause 21 inserts a new part 6B in the Prisons Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Section 59K of the new part 6B allows the Commissioner of Prisons to release eligible inmates on the EmPS.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clause 25 repeals section 81 of the Prisons Act, which provides for the WRS.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The EmPS will adopt a step-down approach to gradually ease inmates back into the society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Emplacement starts with the in-camp phase where eligible and suitable inmates serve the tail-end of their imprisonment sentence in a work release centre administered by SPS.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The inmates may work, upskill themselves through training, or pursue their education, outside prison during the day.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: They will return to reside at the work release centre in the evening.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Inmates who show good progress during the in-camp phase will be permitted to move on to the weekend home leave phase, during which they can return to their place of residence during the weekends.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: If inmates continue to demonstrate good progress during the weekend home leave phase, they can return to their place of residence daily after work, classes or training, under the long home leave phase.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Factors such as their progress and response to rehabilitation, family support and risk of re-offending will be considered.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: All eligible inmates will be assessed by SPS for their suitability.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: All suitable cases will then be surfaced to an independent advisory committee appointed by the Minister for Home Affairs, which will review the cases and make its recommendations to the Commissioner.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clause 26 of the Bill provides for the establishment, function and procedure of this committee via regulations made pursuant to the Prisons Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Commissioner, taking into consideration the committee’s recommendation, may then emplace an inmate on the EmPS.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Inmates on the EmPS will be under SPS's supervision and will receive support for their reintegration.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Besides requiring the inmates to be employed, undergo skills training or education, inmates will be subjected to conditions such as electronic monitoring, mandatory reporting and curfew hours.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: These EmPS conditions are similar to the existing conditions for the HDS and External Placement Scheme, or EPS.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We will also introduce additional conditions for the EmPS, HDS and EPS to better facilitate SPS' administration of the schemes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: First, clauses 12, 17 and 21 insert two new conditions for inmates on the HDS, EPS and home leave phase of the EmPS.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The cost of electronic monitoring would continue to be borne by SPS.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Inmates on these schemes are required to abide by all stipulated conditions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Under clause 21, if an inmate on the EmPS is suspected to have violated any condition or committed any offence, he may be recalled to prison pending SPS' inquiry.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: If found to have breached any condition or committed any offence, the inmate may have his emplacement order revoked.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clauses 13, 14, 18 and 19 expand the scope of recall to prison and revocation of an emplacement order to include the commission of any offence, not just prison offences, by inmates on the HDS or EPS.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This is to deter inmates from re-offending and allow SPS to take swift action against inmates who commit any offence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: If an inmate on the EmPS commits a prison offence and he is punished with confinement in a punishment cell or with forfeiture of his period of remission or both, SPS will have discretion in suspending the inmate's emplacement order.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In contrast, it is mandatory under the current provisions for the HDS and EPS for SPS to suspend the inmate's emplacement order and recall him to prison.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This could be disruptive to the inmate's reintegration, including his studies or work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Hence, clauses 15 and 20 align the provisions for all three schemes such that it is discretionary, not mandatory, to suspend the emplacement orders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This will allow a more calibrated approach to be taken based on the facts of the case.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Next, clauses 10, 12, 17 and 21 expand the means by which the Commissioner may notify persons on the MAS, HDS, EPS and EmPS of changes to the conditions that they are subject to.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Presently, the law requires a written notification of changes to the conditions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: To enhance administrative flexibility and efficiency, alternative means using SMS and other digital communications, will be introduced and these will be prescribed via regulations made pursuant to the Prisons Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Next, I will speak about the amendments facilitating SPS' operations and administration.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Today, inmates sentenced to imprisonment would generally be released after they have served two-thirds of their sentence, if they had displayed good conduct and behaviour in prison.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: When they are released, they will be issued with a Conditional Remission Order which will be valid until the end of their sentence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This period is also known as the "remission period".

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Currently, section 50I(3) of the Prisons Act allows the Commissioner to delay the making of a remission order by up to two weeks.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In other words, the inmate may be detained for up to two weeks into the remission period to carry out any outstanding Court-ordered punishment, typically caning.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For avoidance of doubt, the Commissioner does not have the power to defer an inmate's release beyond the Court-imposed imprisonment sentence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This two-week period may sometimes be insufficient as an inmate may file a Notice of Appeal within two weeks, or 14 days, after the date of the sentence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Under section 327 of the Criminal Procedure Code, the caning ordered by the Court must not be carried out until after the expiration of the 14-day period for filing the Notice of Appeal.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Hence, even if no Notice of Appeal is filed, the earliest that SPS will carry out the Court-ordered caning is after the 14-day period.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Courts, at times, may backdate an imprisonment sentence with caning for an inmate who had served a period of remand as the remand period is counted towards the fulfilment of the sentence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In such a scenario, an inmate may be due for release within 14 days of sentencing.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: SPS would then need to seek a Court order under section 326 of the Criminal Procedure Code to authorise the detention of the inmate for as long as it is reasonably necessary for the caning to be carried out.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This is because, as I mentioned earlier, the Prisons Act currently allows an inmate's release to be delayed by up to two weeks only.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: All the cases were due to the backdating of sentences.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: SPS will release the inmate as soon as the caning has been carried out and he is certified fit for release.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Again, for avoidance of doubt, the Commissioner does not have the power to defer an inmate's release beyond the Court-imposed imprisonment sentence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Next, clause 26 allows the Minister for Home Affairs to make additional regulations related to inmates' communications to uphold the security and good order of the prison.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Currently, there are no restrictions as to whether a person can publish or disseminate information obtained via any form of communication with an inmate.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In addition, SPS can only withhold certain letters sent by or to inmates if they contain anything that affects the security or good order of the prison.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We propose two amendments to improve the current security regime.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Persons who give this undertaking should not publish or disseminate, or cause to be published or disseminated, any information contained in any communication with an inmate that may firstly, affect the security or good order of the prison; or secondly, incite the commission of any offence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Examples of information that may affect the security or good order of the prison include drawings of the prison layout, information related to the security installations of a prison and coded messages for starting a prison disturbance.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: An example of inciting the commission of any offence is instigating inmates to riot or harm another inmate or person.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: SPS has previously intercepted secret society-related messages in letters sent by or to inmates.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Sometimes, the messages were sent in coded form.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Such messages, if let through, could lead to clashes among inmates who are aligned to different secret societies and undermine the good order or security of the prison, or even incite acts of violence, such as causing hurt to another person outside prison.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The intent of allowing the Minister for Home Affairs to make such regulations is to maintain prison security and ensure the safe and secure custody of inmates.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: It is not the intent to curtail inmates' communication or prevent them from airing grievances.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Bona fide communications will not be redacted or withheld.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For Members' information, there are various channels for inmates to provide feedback.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: They can raise concerns to the Superintendent of the prison or any SPS officer.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Inmates can also give feedback directly to members of the Board of Visiting Justices.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Appointed by the Minister for Home Affairs, the Visiting Justices conduct unannounced inspections of the prisons and hear issues raised by inmates.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: These issues are documented, followed up by SPS and the outcomes will be reported back to the Board.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Next, clause 24 updates and provides clarity on prison offences by repealing and re-enacting sections 72 and 73 of the Prisons Act, which list minor and aggravated prison offences respectively.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In practice, SPS does not enforce against these offences.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Work programmes in prison are voluntary in nature.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: If, after choosing to participate in a work programme, an inmate idles, refuses to work or is negligent in his work, he will simply be taken off the work programme, with no disciplinary action taken against him.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Similarly, if an inmate refuses to undergo medical treatment and his medical condition or injury is serious, he will be conveyed to a hospital for further observation and treatment, with no disciplinary action taken against him.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: With more inmates emplaced in the community over time, it is opportune to provide more clarity on applicable prison offences.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clause 24 will specify that certain prison offences are not applicable when an inmate is serving his imprisonment sentence outside prison.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: An example of a prison offence that is not applicable to inmates who are not in prison would be tampering with prison locks.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Currently, there are only prison offences prescribed in the Prisons Act for the HDS but not these two schemes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This amendment seeks to standardise the prison offences across these three community-based programmes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Next, clause 25 provides prison officers with powers to compel the production of documents or information for investigating breaches of conditions and commission of prison offences.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Prison officers conduct inquiries to ascertain if a minor breach of a mandatory aftercare condition, a breach of any of the conditions of community-based programmes such as the HDS or EPS or a prison offence had been committed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: There were instances where prison officers faced difficulties in obtaining pertinent information from external parties to ascertain if a breach had been committed – for example, CCTV footage to prove curfew breaches.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: It is an offence if anyone, without reasonable excuse, fails to provide the required document or information.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Next, clause 25 protects prison officers and Auxiliary Police Officers, or APOs, from liability for acts and omissions done in good faith and with reasonable care, under the Prisons Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In their daily duties, prison officers sometimes have to take calculated risks and make prompt decisions to maintain the safe and secure custody of inmates.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For example, a prison officer escorting an inmate outside of prison, may use any weapon on any person or inmate who tries to force open a prison transport vehicle to facilitate an inmate's escape.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In the course of preventing the escape, the prison officer's actions may cause injury to others or damage property.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Under the Prisons Act and Misuse of Drugs Act, APOs may also be employed by the Commissioner of Prisons to assist SPS in escorting and guarding inmates.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: It is worth noting that it is explicitly stated that prison officers and APOs are protected from legal liability if they had acted in good faith and with reasonable care under the Misuse of Drugs Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: However, this is not the case for the Prisons Act, although they are protected under the common law defence of necessity.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This is in line with what is provided for Police officers in the Police Force Act and SCDF officers in the Civil Defence Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: To be clear, officers are not exempt from the ordinary process of law if they have abused their powers or are criminally negligent.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Next, we will update the terminology used in the Prisons Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clause 7 replaces all references to "leprosy" with "infectious disease" in section 45(2) of the Prisons Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This will allow the Minister for Home Affairs to direct the removal of any inmate suffering from any infectious disease, not just leprosy, to any hospital or any specified place for treatment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In practice, SPS does not discriminate against inmates with leprosy.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: All inmates with or suspected of having infectious diseases, including leprosy, have ample access to healthcare and treatment services.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Next, the Bill will grant administrative flexibility to SPS.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clause 4 allows the Minister for Home Affairs to appoint more than one Deputy Commissioner of Prisons who can exercise and perform the Commissioner's powers, duties and functions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Currently, only one Deputy Commissioner of Prisons can be appointed under the Prisons Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clause 4 also allows the Commissioner of Prisons to delegate any of his or her powers, duties and functions under any written law, instead of those under the Prisons Act only, to any of the Deputy Commissioners, Divisional Directors and Cluster Commanders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: An example of the Commissioner’s powers under any written law is the appointment of day reporting officers under section 341(7) of the Criminal Procedure Code.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Lastly, clause 3 allows the Minister for Home Affairs to appoint places as temporary lock-ups.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Currently, the Minister for Home Affairs may appoint lock-ups only at Police stations and Court houses, for the confinement of persons arrested, awaiting trial, remanded, or sentenced to an imprisonment term of up to a month.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In the event where there is a mass arrest, such as during a public order incident, it would be operationally expedient to hold all of the arrested persons in a centralised lock-up, rather than across multiple lock-ups.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This would facilitate security, investigations and post-event actions, including prosecution.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: To ensure that we can call up additional capacity when needed, clause 3 allows the Minister for Home Affairs to appoint other places that are not Police stations or Court houses as temporary lock-ups for the confinement of persons.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The amendments in the Bill will help to improve inmates’ rehabilitation and reintegration outcomes and enable SPS to be more effective in carrying out its work.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: All Singaporeans expect that if one were to commit a crime, he or she will have to pay the price irrespective of one’s individual background.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The force of deterrence is high because the application of justice is swift and sure.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But the arm of the law is also one that reaches beyond the prison sentence.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It aims to rehabilitate and welcome ex-prisoners back to society.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is a strong signal that we do not give up on those who have made mistakes.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The excellent work that Singapore Prison Service (SPS) officers do as "Captains of Lives" is perhaps not as well-known.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In collaboration with its partners, SPS works to: enforce the safe and secure custody of prisoners; deliver evidence-informed rehabilitation programmes; and carry out effective community supervision of released offenders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: All these are to help prisoners find their way back to society, into families, friendship and work.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These hard-earned results are due, in part, to a number of innovative steps that SPS has implemented over the years to help rehabilitate and reintegrate ex-offenders into our society.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Minister of State has outlined these steps which were taken over two decades, in particular.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I will not repeat the steps that the hon Minister of State had said.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But what is clear is that prison is not mere punishment for wrongdoing.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is also the first step towards education, reconciliation and the acquisition of requisite skills and knowledge.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is to enable ex-offenders to become financially independent and confident of their abilities and then have fulfilling lives and careers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They will be able to re-assume their responsibilities for themselves and their families.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They will have a chance to leave their chequered past behind, be reintegrated back with their families, society and make positive contributions to our country.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: With our help, they can rebuild their lives, step by courageous step.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is a mission that requires stout-hearted support from everyone.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am proud of my alma mater, NUS, whose professors interviewed a prison inmate, as part of its rigorous admission process and offered him a spot in its Law School.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Today, that man is a litigation lawyer and both of us are fellow members of the same profession serving our country.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Employers must be open-minded in the same way.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The main reason why I suggested in Parliament in 2020 that the $1 billion Jobs Growth Initiative (JGI), which sought to expand local hiring during the pandemic by providing wage support, be also extended to ex-offenders was because I was concerned that, with the shrinking economy then, employers may not offer our ex-offenders with fair chances of getting good employment.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This, in turn, would have had a major impact on the rehabilitative process for our ex-offenders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Government adopted my suggestion and addressed the issue squarely.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is for the same reasons that I strongly support the Employment Preparation Scheme (EmPS) which is aimed at improving the employability of our prison inmates.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I have studied the details of the scheme as set out in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Collectively, the measures provide a suite of levers to our SPS officers to ensure inmates stay the course so as to obtain skills and knowledge necessary to get good jobs while they are serving their sentences.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is by no means a simple matter, but the odds are good, so long as they put in the effort.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I have one question on the working of the EmPS.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The schemes I have in mind are the Home Detention Scheme, Conditional Remission System and the Mandatory Aftercare Scheme.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It seems likely that many inmates in these existing schemes will also want to benefit from the employability feature under EmPS.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Minister of State took some pains to explain the reasons why this amendment is being proposed and he made it clear that it is not suggested that the Commissioner would be able to extend the imprisonment term of the inmate beyond what is ordered by the Courts.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The point I am concerned about is slightly different.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The way the Remission Orders System works, there is a legitimate expectation on the part of the inmates that they would be released so long as they do not behave badly.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, they would get a one-third remission of the sentence.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Given that state of play, the concern I have is whether there could be a possible conflict of interest that may arise when a Commissioner extends the period of time to issue the remission order such that there is, in a sense, a delay.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I appreciate that the reason for this is because there is a need to carry out the corporal punishment.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Under the Prisons Act, SPS has the ability to actually forfeit a period of remission of up to 180 days.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I looked at the Hansard, I could not find the reason.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Therefore, I would be indebted to the hon Minister of State if he could explain the matter.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In 2014, the hon Member Mr Christopher de Souza, on the occasion of the Second Reading of the Prisons (Amendment) Bill then, recounted the lyrics of the well-known song, "Tie a Yellow Ribbon Round the Old Oak Tree" as being the inspiration for the Yellow Ribbon Project.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: His speech has inspired me to, not to sing the song, but to recount the lyrics of a local song, “I Ain’t Giving Up” written by Mr Steven Joseph and performed by Mr Zulkifli Rahman, Mr Razif Haron and Mr Affandi Meskam.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Talented musicians, they took the opportunity to learn music formally when they were serving sentence and pursued their dreams upon release.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The chorus goes like this: I ain't giving up up up I'm gonna find my way I ain't giving up up up No matter what they say For the love you've given Won't need another reason To ride on, fight on And lead on, hey!

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Their music is their story, and the stories and hopes of many more.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I have a suggestion for the hon Minister for Defence.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I know they will give any professional musician a run for their money.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I also know that they will make Singaporeans rise to their feet.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Most importantly, this will be our nation’s signal to our prison inmates who have served their time that, as a community, we will do what it takes to support them in their rehabilitation and reintegration journey.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So long as they do not give up, we too, do not give up, we too, will help each other to find our way back.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I do not oppose the Bill but will raise some questions for clarification as well as a few suggestions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Most of us would agree that prisoners should not be treated cruelly or inhumanely and that as a society, we should do our utmost to reintegrate ex-prisoners into the societal mainstream after they have paid their debt to society.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This is a step in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It helps to reintegrate prisoners into society when they are ultimately released.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It helps them to build up some relevant skills and some form of financial cushion for that time and also helps provide local workers for our economy, hopefully enabling us to reduce some dependence on foreign workers, which is a positive thing, for reasons I have articulated in past speeches in this House, notably during the debate on CECA.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Such company partnerships should have a skilling element whilst at the same time, incorporating fair wages similar to traineeships, where workers are developed rather than being treated solely as sources of cheap labour.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, community reintegration involves not just the economic aspect of living in the community.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Can we also provide support services for after prison life?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There are pastoral care services, especially with volunteers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Some of these pastoral care services are now provided by prison officers on rotation from enforcement duties in addition to the rehabilitation officers who are clearly already involved in pastoral care service.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This could help build restorative relationships between inmates and officers, but may also help and I quote, "may also help officers avoid the damage they experience by performing purely punitive functions", to quote from a report on ex-prisoner reintegration around the world.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Anecdotally, it appears that they may still be issues being faced here, notwithstanding the collaboration between the SPS and POSB that was started in 2015 to facilitate the setting up of bank accounts by ex-offenders upon release from prison.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, Madam, I would like to clarify some points relating to the EMPS.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Work release schemes have been in existence since 1985.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Since that time, so as to quantify and assess the link between these employment schemes and the welfare of prisoners, as well as recidivism rates post-release, has the Ministry been monitoring the following things.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Some ex-inmates report that they are only able to use their work income to buy things within the prison, but I am not sure if this is indeed the case now.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Thirdly, the proportion of inmates who have participated in such schemes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And fourthly, the impact of prison work programmes on recidivism.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There may be an argument for not paying our workers on such schemes a full salary as they would earn outside prison, which is part of the punitive aspect of imprisonment, but work programmes like the EMPS should be structured to ensure that: firstly, companies using prison labour are not unfairly benefiting from the low costs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We should recall that some of these inmates may have worked far higher paid jobs and already have skills that are highly valued outside the prison environment; and secondly, labour should come at a cost that is in some way, benchmarked to minimum wage equivalence, so that inmates have some sort of savings buffer when they leave.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: They should not re-enter society at a huge financial disadvantage because this is a reason why many inmates commit crimes in the first place.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And if not, would the Government consider introducing such protections by way of subsidiary legislation or by some other means?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Such inmate workers may be at the risk of exploitation, given that they do not sign contracts of service.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, Madam, I would like to seek some clarifications regarding the eligibility criteria for employment under the new section 59 of the Act and this is something that the hon Minister of State, Dr Faishal Ibrahim, spoke about at some length.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Does an inmate apply or are all eligible inmates, that is, those who have served at least 14 days of imprisonment, automatically considered for this?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Any decision by the SPS appears to be final.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: What safeguards are there to ensure that these decisions are impartial and fair?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Would the Ministry consider an alternative approach whereby all eligible cases, provided there is no prohibitive circumstance that can be clearly spelled out and filtered for, are automatically referred to the independent advisory committee for consideration for EMPS without the need for the SPS to refer prisoners to the committee as it were.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, one of the factors considered by the commissioner is the degree to which the inmate enjoys family support and this was reiterated earlier by the Minister of State.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This factor is referred to in the first footnote of MHA's press release on this Bill.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Does this prejudice inmates who unfortunately do not have sufficient family support in respect of being able to participate in employment preparation?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Could more be done in ensuring that those who enjoy less family support be included in the EMPS as well?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, being allowed to stay in special shelters while participating in employment preparation and to be assigned mentors.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It may be that inmates with less family support are, other things being equal, more at risk of unsuccessfully reintegrating into society than those with ample family support.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Inmates currently have access to "N", "O" and "A" level courses alongside the Ngee Ann Polytechnic Diploma in Business Practice for International Supply Chain Management.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Recently, I understand that SUSS has launched a part-time degree programme the prison inmates can participate in and there could be other educational and training programmes that they have access to as well.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, can prisoners be allowed to take part in Polytechnic diploma courses related to future-ready economic sectors, or to entrepreneurship and innovation?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I would suggest that this could include courses offered by private companies to obtain certification in very specific types of skills, like coding, for example.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I would also like to ask the Government if inmates are able to take up these courses at subsidised rates.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Also, if they were to complete their studies and after release, secure a job and do not demonstrate recidivism for certain period of time, would the Government consider a scheme whereby their student debts or part of your student debts can be forgiven?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Such a scheme would incentivise inmates to take up courses of study while in prison and may also play some role in reducing recidivism, given the substantial literature that suggests a link between criminal activity and financial distress.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And on that note, I would also like to suggest that financial literacy training should also be included in the training provided to ex-offenders before release to ensure better personal financial management, which I suspect could help lower recidivism rates.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Perhaps MoneySense, the national financial education programme, could be brought in to play a role here.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: All these measures are important in tackling recidivism.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: As a society, there is still much to do to tackle the risk of recidivism.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, Madam, let me move on to some concerns and clarifications related to the new powers in this Bill enabling SPS to redact or withhold inmates' correspondence and curtailing what visitors can say publicly about their visits to the prison.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Of course, they can take guidance from the examples of information listed in footnote 5 to the MHA press release and reiterated by Minister of State Dr Faishal Ibrahim, but that does not appear to be exhaustive.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Could the Minister of State provide more details of the kinds of information that would run afoul of this provision?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Would the Minister of State also confirm that a visitor disseminating information that is factually correct and does not correspond to these categories of information, of which the examples have been given, would not run afoul of this provision?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, factually correct information about a prisoner having suffered injuries.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This provision gives the Minister for Home Affairs power to make regulations to redact or withhold inmates' correspondence that may affect the security or good order of prisons or incite the commission of any offence.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This provision appears to be in line with section 127A of the Prisons Regulations.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Prima facie, this provision has implications for the freedom of speech of inmates.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Freedom of speech is protected by Article 14 of the Singapore Constitution although as it stands, it is a qualified right.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The Constitution provides that Parliament may by law impose such restrictions as it considers necessary or expedient in the interest of the security of Singapore or any part thereof, or in relation to the incitement to commit any offence.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This provision confers on the Minister powers to make restrictions on inmates' correspondence that appears to be in line with the qualifications on the freedom of speech provided for in the Constitution, that is, security of the prison and incitement to commit offences.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But the question remains whether this provision is a proportionate response to the problem it seeks to solve.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In this spirit, while I do not object to the provision in question, I would like to ask for more guidance as to how these powers will be used.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, this provision does not seem to provide an exception for letters written to a prisoner's legal advisor, unlike section 127A of the Regulations.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: My purpose in raising this point is not to argue that correspondence relating to, say, a planned prison breakout, for example, should be exempt from this provision if it is between a lawyer and his client.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But it would be useful if the Government can clarify the status of legal communication under this provision.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And on that note, it is also unclear if prisoners will be notified if their letters are redacted or withheld and I would like to seek clarity on this point from MHA.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is also unclear what is the review or appeal mechanism should the Minister exercise this power.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: If so, what form would the appeals process take?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I think the answer to my question must surely be no, as everything I have read about this Bill suggests, but I would like to have that answered all the same.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A few years ago, I was given the opportunity to engage with girls undergoing reformative training.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A group of volunteers and I shared with them practical tips and life skills such as budgeting, how to go about applying for school or a job.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And some of them shared how nobody had ever sat with them like that, listening to their thoughts, offering advice when appropriate and personalising next steps depending on what best suited them.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When they came out, we would meet with our girls and all of them would express similar regrets and also new resolve – to change, to do better, both for themselves and their families.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, many feared that past decisions would continue to follow them like a stain caused by indelible ink throughout their lives.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Offenders serve time after committing their wrongdoings, but often their families – spouses, parents, young children – are punished too.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And this punishment can continue unless we unlock the second prison in society.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In 2021, I have spoken about similar issues, such as assistance for inmates’ families and support for youth offenders, and I am heartened that more steps are being taken to enhance the rehabilitative process as it is a critical step in helping inmates – and their families – to reintegrate and in time contribute to society.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The expansion of the Work Release Scheme to also include educational and upskilling opportunities is important.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Studies consistently show that education while carrying out one’s sentence improves an inmate’s post-release employment outcomes and reduces recidivism rates.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Similarly, in Australia, a 2018 study found that inmates who successfully completed vocational education and training programmes were 2.5 times more likely to remain out of prison after two years.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The EmPS takes things one step further by allowing inmates to access educational opportunities they would otherwise not have been able to take advantage of while serving their sentence.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singapore Prison Services (SPS) has also been expanding its rehabilitation efforts in recent years.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The EmPS underscores SPS’ commitment towards rehabilitation as a sentencing principle and will complement these efforts.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: That said, I hope to seek some clarifications on the Bill.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First is with regard to the available opportunities under the EmPS.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What kinds of jobs, education and upskilling programmes will be available to inmates?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Do the nature of these jobs differ from those offered under the Work Release Scheme?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How do we ensure that work environments are conducive for rehabilitation and minimise the chance of recidivism?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Beyond just jobs, would these educational opportunities only be limited to vocational training, or will they also include academic programmes for those who may desire to do so?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that a broader scope of upskilling opportunities to keep pace with the workforce of the future would be considered.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Second is on eligibility and progression through the scheme.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I note that the EmPS consists of three phases: the in-camp phase, the weekend home leave phase and the long home leave phase.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What is the intended duration of each phase?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If progress to the next phase is decided on a case-by-case basis, what are some of the criteria used in this decision?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With respect to the in-camp phase and work release centre, I understand that Institution S2 at the Selarang Park Complex, which is run by SPS, is currently the only facility designated as a work release centre.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will there be sufficient space for suitable offenders to participate in the programme, or will other spaces be created in due course?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, one of the criteria mentioned in the Bill for eligibility of the programme is the level of family support an inmate has.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And in fact, it could be poor familial ties which had caused them to offend in the first place.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, that does not mean that they do not have the heart, nor the will, to complete the programme.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that some flexibility, on a carefully considered case-by-case basis where deserving and appropriate, can be granted in the long home leave phase or other appropriate accommodation be considered.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Next, while enhancing the employment opportunities is important, staying employed, retaining employment and being relevant are just as important.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I understand that the Yellow Ribbon Project does have career coaching, career guidance and job facilitation programmes but not all offenders may be aware of or know how to take up these support schemes meaningfully.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Government consider allocating resources for coaches, for example, for the medium-term to support these ex-offenders for an appropriate period of time after release?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They can also help them with administrative and logistical matters such as registering for lost ICs or setting up bank accounts.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This would increase the chances of job retention after placement and employment in the long run to provide stability for ex-offenders and their families.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, some face financial difficulties or even debt from the day of release.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would there be any educational support stipends considered to support them as they take up opportunities under EmPS?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Lastly, while the EmPS might better equip inmates with workforce-ready skillsets, on its own, it cannot change employers and colleagues' perceptions of and sometimes prejudice against, ex-offenders.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The work to manage negative societal attitudes is endless, but I do hope and urge those in and out of the House today, to address any personal prejudices that we might come across to help unlock the second prison.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am very blessed to have a mixed pool of volunteers on the ground, some of whom have served their time, some of whom we met through the Yellow Ribbon Project actually and then decided to spend their time volunteering.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many share that in the past, it was always someone else visiting them and their families and that helped them along in their journeys.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Allowing them to cultivate stronger ties with their neighbours and own communities on the ground gives them a chance to see things from a different perspective, make amends and to feel like they too can have purpose and help others.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am very grateful when they choose to step forward despite curious glances at tagging bracelets, difficult conversations about where they have been for the past few months and even more grateful when they manage to stay the course.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that society and more community organisations will give them a chance to become volunteers and in time, community leaders, perhaps, when it is possible to do so safely.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My last point on the Bill is regarding the amendment on regulations to redact or withhold inmates’ correspondence to maintain prison security.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is without a doubt vitally important for SPS to ensure the integrity and security of prison systems.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, I would like to ask about possible unintended consequences of this amendment.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the context of COVID-19, when face-to-face visits have been suspended from volunteers and family members, letters have been all the more important as a form of personalised communication between inmates and their families and as a pillar of support.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, a pregnant mom trying to reach out to her husband who is an inmate, or a daughter in prison trying to find out more about her elderly ill parents.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the processing time of written correspondence between inmates and their families be affected?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Malay):   Mdm Deputy Speaker, I rise in support of this Bill which steps up efforts to rehabilitate and reintegrate ex-inmates back into society.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Through the EmPS, ex-inmates can enhance their skills and education for their future after being released from prison.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will open up more opportunities to explore other sectors of employment or education.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, apart from them undergoing upskilling courses or seeking employment through EmPS, I am also concerned whether they are burdened by the lack of savings or money for expenses.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Although family support is very important, we also recognise that not all ex-convicts have family support or enough savings for their daily expenses or to continue their education.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition to our support towards the rehabilitation and integration efforts of inmates, can the Government also look at how they can be given some form of financial assistance and receive guidance after their release so that they do not face any hardship in their daily expenses?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): Mdm Deputy Speaker, overall, I am heartened that this Bill equips inmates with more opportunities to upskill and seek meaningful employment.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It also introduces practical measures to increase the efficiency and effectiveness of SPS’ operations.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Notwithstanding the above clarifications, I believe that these amendments will bring about benefits to society as a whole.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Besides rehabilitating them, it also helps to raise inmates’ employability, in line with our national upskilling endeavours.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This new pool of trained employees will help to alleviate manpower shortages.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, Mdm Deputy Speaker, there is the need to ensure participation from genuine employers for the programme to succeed.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will there also be an appropriate industry body that accredits and matches potential employers?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Ideally, these employers should meet relevant criteria or have a track record for rehabilitating and hiring ex-offenders.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: On the other hand, if the demands and requirements imposed on potential employers are too onerous, employers are unlikely to take part.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is important to establish a balance between the interests of employers and the participating ex-offenders.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A myriad of factors will be taken into account, to ensure a good match between the workplace and the employee.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Briefings and ongoing support for employers and staff are provided before and during the placement.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will the Ministry or SPS likewise conduct similar placement assessments?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Besides the employers, are the employees aware that they will be working with an inmate?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can employers count on our programme administrators for clear regulations and reliable support?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Support can also come in the form of training for employers and managers on working with ex-offenders.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Ex-offenders tend to carry emotional baggage and carry a stigma.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Some believe that they are constantly being judged.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Unpleasant events, like being criticised by their supervisor or customer, can trigger adverse reactions or discourage them.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Employers should have timely access to support from prison counsellors to help with such situations.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Employers who abuse the system or refuse to abide by the regulations are a potential concern.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There are always errant employers who exploit the schemes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They may join the programme to benefit from the grants or positive publicity.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: On the flip side, they may not have a proper training plan or work arrangement for the participant.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A first poor employment experience can be disheartening for inmates.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It deprives them of a valuable integration opportunity.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: So, there should be regulations and penalties for errant employers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Ministry also clarify whether remuneration for inmates will be managed by SPS?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Or will remuneration be paid by the employers to the prisoner directly?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Does SPS allocate the upskilling and training opportunities, or do the eligible participants have to source for the opportunities themselves?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Are there plans to engage more employers to come onboard?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: With the expansion of the programme, how will the additional costs and resources be defrayed?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For EmPS to be successful, exemplary discipline of the participant inmate is important.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I am glad that the Bill has drawn up very detailed conditions of the employment preparation order.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As a matter of deterrence, besides including the residual discretion of the Commissioner of Prisons to include conditions as the Commissioner deemed fit, it should be explicitly stated what participants are prohibited from doing.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is because some employers worry about vice and problematic behaviour, such as gangsterism and gambling among ex-offenders.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is especially if the participant inmates were formerly convicted of the said crimes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Having this clause will help allay their concerns.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is not to stigmatise the inmates, but to provide clarity and assurance to all involved parties.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While Singaporeans in general approve of second chances for ex-offenders who are rehabilitated, the "Not in my back yard" syndrome, or NIMBY, can be apparent in this case.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Whilst some agree on the need to train and rehabilitate ex-offenders into society, that does not necessarily translate into willingness of oneself to attend classes or work in the same workplace with them.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: So, I seek clarification on whether participating inmates will attend classes together with the public?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If so, will there be ways to remove identifiers associated with the participating inmates, such as not requiring the wearing of prison attire, or wearing electronic tracking devices at a spot where it is not visible?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Government also clarify on the types of inmates who are eligible for EmPS?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Do they include serious offences already set out in the Second Schedule of the Prisons Act (Cap 247) like drug trafficking, culpable homicide not amounting to murder, or sexual offences and other violent crimes?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I understand that all eligible inmates will be assessed by SPS for their suitability for the programme.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There will be an independent advisory committee appointed by MHA to review the cases and make recommendations to the Commissioner.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I believe that the eligible candidates would have proven themselves worthy.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Nonetheless, can the Ministry assure the public that there is no risk of the inmate offending or causing harm while on EmPS?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What steps will the Ministry take to mitigate such risks?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Sometimes, a person’s discrimination against others can stem from past trauma.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For example, a former victim of sexual assault with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) may feel unsafe to spend time in the same space as a convicted sex offender.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This further drives the point of the difficulty and necessity to balance the needs of the public.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Is it not better to adjust the grace period so the prisoner receives the punishment during his incarceration, rather than extend his sentence?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is understood that such prisoners often have a grace period and their sentences are backdated, so there is no time to deal the punishment while they serve their sentence.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, durations of appeal can prolong the process, such that 21 days may not even be adequate.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Employment and job search are top pain points for these residents.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Wariness from employers, discrimination from the public and a lack of suitable skills are the key hurdles.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The expanded EmPS would address some of these issues.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This can be done with a proper framework that formalises their obligations and access to support from SPS.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It should clarify the prohibitions of participants under the EmPS, which would serve as deterrence and give employers added assurance of good behaviour.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It should also take into consideration concerns from the public and minimise prejudice to give inmates a chance to prove themselves.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Currently, inmates at the tail-end of their sentence are allowed to work in the community under the Work Release Scheme (WRS), which helps to ease their transition into society under gainful employment.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: However, if these inmates have been in prison for a long period of time, they may find it hard to find a job as the job market would have evolved significantly.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: If this is left unaddressed, the skills mismatch would result in low employment rates.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: However, despite our best efforts, there will still be those who re-offend, even if they are placed in proper jobs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Are there any lessons that can be applied to EmPS to help further reduce recidivism rates?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Ten years ago, the iPhone 5 has just gone into the market and its maximum storage of 64GB then felt more than sufficient.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Today, we have the iPhone 13 with a whopping storage capacity of 1TB.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Technologies such as mobile payments and 5G technology will seem foreign to inmates who have been incarcerated for a lengthy period.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: What are the efforts to help such prisoners reintegrate back into society?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Can we have digital ambassadors to provide technology familiarisation sessions so that we can better prepare these inmates for the new environment outside of the prison?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
