text: The Labour Movement, through the Employment and Employability Institute (e2i) and our Job Security Council, has been actively partnering the Yellow Ribbon Singapore to match ex-offenders with available jobs in the market.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I hope that the relevant authorities will continue to review such restrictions and exercise more flexibility so that we can help our ex-offenders access some of these jobs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Let us reduce the stigma and not let their past actions continue to cast a shadow over their future.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But I hope that more can be done to help ease ex-offenders’ transition into society and reduce the stigmatisation that they face, so that they will feel confident re-entering society and not fall back into a life of crime.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This will supplement the current Community-based Programmes framework or CBPs and help ex-offenders improve their employability and facilitate their reintegration into society.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, we can expect that the new EmPS, together with the CBPs, will lead to a further reduction in recidivism.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: So, MHA and the Singapore Prisons Service really should be commended for not just sitting on their laurels but working to continually improve the system, including with this new EmPS, to try to further lower recidivism rates.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In particular, part 6B section 59K of the amended Act makes provision for inmates "to participate, in any place outside the limits of the prison in which the prisoner is detained, in any educational or occupational training programme, or any other activity for the purpose of facilitating the prisoner to be gainfully employed, that may be specified in the order" and follows with conditions stipulated in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: First, section 59L of the amended Act sets out the Commissioner's considerations as regards whether an offender is suitable for employment preparation.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: On this, I hope that the SPS will adopt a liberal interpretation to the stipulations and that eventually, all but the most recalcitrant or unresponsive of offenders would be eligible for the EmPS and other reintegration schemes.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The reason for this is that incarceration terms inevitably end at some point and effort ought to be made for the rehabilitation and reintegration of offenders even if they have shown themselves to be unresponsive at first.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, it may well be that the offenders who need these schemes most are precisely those who appear less responsive as they may have the most difficulty reintegrating and the highest risk of re-offending.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Second, given our ageing population, the number of elderly ex-offenders returning to society will increase.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Older offenders returning to society may face greater challenges trying to find employment.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: One of the reasons highlighted was their loss of motivation to go for courses or to upgrade their skills.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: One of the study participants was quoted as saying and I read the quote verbatim, "I don't have any skills, no qualifications, no license.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Now, most classes are in English." Another thought is that "I'm already at this age, just pass each day as it is, no motivation to upgrade." In this connection, I urge the SPS and its partners to consider older inmates as a distinct group under the EmPS that may need to develop skills and have employment preparation specific to their age group.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This could help avoid the sense of helplessness some of them feel once they are released, when they are faced with the real pressures of getting a job, being financially independent and, for some of them, having to support members of their family.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: These inmates may need to be on such schemes for a longer period to catch up with skills and to be mentally prepared to return to the workplace.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Our ex-offenders are also part of our Singapore core and we need to make this all-of-society effort to make sure none of us is left behind or left out.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Notwithstanding my clarifications and suggestions, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We are second only to Norway and South Korea.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is an applaudable achievement and a testimony to the good work done by Singapore Prison Service.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given our low penal recidivism rate, the Employment Preparation Scheme (EmPS) is a positive step in the right direction because it seeks to provide inmates better opportunities to reintegrate back to society as they will be allowed to undergo skills training and education as well as working within the community.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With sufficient training and preparation at the tail-end of their sentences, inmates have better chances to be employed upon their release and ultimately, increasing the chances of successful reintegration back to society.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, I would like to seek clarification on a few matters.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Under the previous Work Release Scheme (WRS), inmates were given permission to leave prisons in order to work.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we reduce it, keeping in mind the intent to have more inmates emplaced on the EmPS?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What is the number and percentage of inmates that are expected to be on EmPS?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Are there inmates with specific crimes that will not be allowed to be on EmPS?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What are the guiding principles that help us ascertain which inmates are suitably ready to be emplaced on EmPS?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given that we expect a larger number of inmates participating in this programme and that the administering is done on a case-by-case basis, we can expect that our prison officers will have an increased workload.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Do we currently have sufficient resources to handle the increased load?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What can we do now in order to ensure our rehabilitation officers are adequately supported as we take more steps towards our "prisons without walls" concept?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The EmPS rests on the premise that inmates who are better prepared through training and upskilling can find meaningful employment once their sentence is over.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Meaningful employment would help the ex-inmate reintegrate better and ultimately be accepted as a useful and contributing member of society.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we ensure the inmates experience good quality training that will lead to a higher chance of them landing a job after their sentences?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Are the courses offered under EmPS limited and only available from specific training providers?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If so, what are the types of training that will be made available to the supervisees and how do we choose our training provider partners for EmPS?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While we want to get suitable inmates prepared for their life post-sentence, we must also be mindful not to dishearten these individuals who are intending to change by exposing them to discrimination which will dampen their confidence to reintegrate through meaningful employment.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With that in mind, how do we ensure the staff and fellow trainees at the training centres are prepared to accept these individuals who are trying to turn over a new leaf?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Are there counselling or career guidance sessions available to help our inmates deal with discrimination or stigmatisation?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With more and more training and jobs needing IT or digital skills, if the training or job emplacement requires the supervisees to have access to mobile devices, social media and access to computers, will these devices be provided for in prison?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Is it a cause of concern if inmates have access to such devices?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Will this affect the inmates' time they spend in prison?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Currently, many citizens can use their SkillsFuture Credit for training and upskilling.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Ultimately, we want relevant and updated training and reskilling for our inmates so that they will have a fair chance of landing a job post-sentence and hence increasing the likelihood that they will be meaningfully employed.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must ensure the quality of such training is of a suitable standard.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, it may also be useful if such training or reskilling is accredited or by the end of the training or reskilling programme, our inmates receive some form of certification to help them with future employability.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With the idea of future employability of our post-sentence inmates in mind, how can we get more employers to be part of the programme to work with the inmates?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Ex-inmates face a tough time landing a job, even with proper skills and qualifications.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Despite the best efforts of many inmates who want to turn over a new leaf, discrimination and stigmatisation remains a reality.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can we better incentivise employers to consider employing ex-inmates?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What can we do to encourage a more welcoming environment for ex-offenders in the workplace?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can EmPS be used to address manpower shortages that we have in digital, manufacturing and engineering industry or even kickstart talent in a new industry, for example, the electric car repair industry?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I believe this would certainly help our inmates be more future ready and hence, more likely to be meaningfully employed post-sentence.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Malay):   Although EmPs provides a golden opportunity for ex-offenders to seek employment and give back to society, we must not forget the important role of the family in reintegrating offenders back to society.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Families should encourage ex-offenders to participate in rehabilitation sessions so that they can use this opportunity to rebuild their lives.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Indeed, EmPs is an opportunity that should be taken up because it will give ex-offenders time to upgrade themselves by acquiring new skills so that they have a better chance of getting a job after being released from prison.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Family support and encouragement are very important because many ex-offenders face a host of challenges as they try to reintegrate into society.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Therefore, we should build a conducive environment for ex-offenders to better themselves and return as members of society who contribute to community and family.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Families will be connected to the necessary assistance network while their spouses who are in prison are given proper support with in-care services.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I previously shared in this House the inspirational stories I heard from ex-offenders and how “family” was the one word they used most frequently in their stories.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I also spoke about how I strongly believe that strengthening family ties is important to improve the rehabilitation process for inmates.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am supportive of the amendments in this Bill, which not only sends a signal about the focus on rehabilitation, but also provides a concrete framework for achieving it.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point is about eligibility for employment preparation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can Minister share at what stage of the imprisonment would the Commissioner assess a prisoner’s suitability for employment?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Should a prisoner be initially assessed as unsuitable, when will the prisoner next be re-assessed?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point is about the categorisation of prison offences.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The new sections 72 and 73 set out minor and aggravated prison offences.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, it is a minor prison offence to carry out any “act, conduct, disorder or neglect to the prejudice of good order or discipline in the prison”.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To help clarify the differences between minor and aggravated prison offences, can Minister provide examples of acts that would fall under the catch-all minor and aggravated prison offences?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can Minister also clarify if the Superintendent has final authority in determining whether the offences committed is a minor or aggravated prison offences and whether the Commissioner has the authority to disagree with the Superintendent’s categorisation of an offence as a minor or aggravated offence?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third and final point is about exceptions to prison offences.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Ministry has said the new Employment Preparation Scheme will include an in-camp phase during which inmates may work or study outside prison during the day and return to reside at a “work release centre” in the evening.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can Minister clarify if prison offences conducted at work, study and residence locations under the scheme would be deemed to be within prison?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is significant, as certain prison offences do not apply to prisoners serving their sentence outside prison.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Would it no longer be an aggravated prison offence for a prisoner to assault another prisoner while working together outside the prison under this scheme?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In summary, I hope Minister can clarify my points on assessing a prisoner’s eligibility for employment preparation, determining the severity of prison offences and providing exceptions to prison offences.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Upon release, reintegration is the most crucial step and post-release employment is critical to the success of an ex-offender’s reintegration into society.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Employment Preparation Scheme can effectively facilitate this.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The proposed scheme is more comprehensive than the Work Release Scheme.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Inmates will be able to equip themselves with relevant skillsets, enhancing their post-release employability.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Retraining is especially crucial, especially considering the pandemic economy.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I will speak on two key areas: the structure of the scheme and the importance of a coordinated, holistic support framework.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: On the scheme itself, I would like to highlight three points: the need to include as many inmates as possible under it, ensuring quality programmes and the provision of financial support for inmates under the scheme.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: First, we must seek to include as many eligible inmates into the scheme as possible.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Inmates are emplaced into the scheme through a two-tier selection process.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Thereafter, they are assessed by an independent advisory committee.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, would the Singapore Prisons Short Risk Scale (SPSRS) be used?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Would inmates be told of the assessment criteria so that they can work towards such a programme?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Could the Ministry also clarify at which stage are inmates eligible to be emplaced under this scheme?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, it seems that inmates are generally emplaced on Community-based Programmes at the tail-end of their sentence.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Second, I believe that the long-term effectiveness of the scheme is dependent on the quality of preparation received by the inmates.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The pandemic, coupled with the destruction of digitalisation, has accelerated growth and demise of many industries, jobs and skillsets.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Upon release, some inmates may find themselves with skillsets that may not be practical or useful in this new economy.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Skills audit and career counselling are then essential for successful training and placement.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How can the Ministry work with organisations such as SSG and e2i to prepare inmates?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The success of training is very much dependent on placement.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: And a place-and-train scheme is often preferred because inmates would be training with a clear purpose.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Labour Movement stands ready to work with tripartite partners to support such initiatives.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Thirdly, many ex-offenders need financial support upon release.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Some would prefer to work rather than invest in training and education.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, the importance of reskilling must not be overlooked as it will place them in a better position to secure gainful employment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Could the Ministry provide training allowance to inmates who take up training and education programmes?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is especially important when the inmates can go home in phase two and three of the scheme.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Next, a coordinated, holistic support framework involving all stakeholders must be in place to ensure the long-term effectiveness of the scheme.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: First, the success of the scheme is dependent on employers’ and workplace support.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Employers and the workplace must try to give a second chance to ex-offenders, accepting them as valued members of the workforce.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The number of employers registered with Yellow Ribbon Singapore (YRSG) has been steadily increasing over the years.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, research has reflected that some inmates who are considered as PMETs were unable to find suitable vacancies commensurate with their qualifications.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There is thus a pressing need to rope in more employers in different industries to join as partners of the scheme.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The unions will lend our support to do so.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There may be scope to investigate enhancing the Jobs Growth Initiative (JGI) for ex-offenders.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Could the Ministry consider enhancing the JGI or offering a one-off bonus when an employer hires an inmate upon their completion of the EmPS with the company?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The continuity in employment post-release will ensure a smoother reintegration into society for ex-offenders.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Perhaps, the JGI can be restructured for hires of ex-offenders, with the provision of Government support running for a longer period of time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Labour Movement will continue to provide our support to their initiatives, because ex-offenders are and can be productive and committed workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The long-term effectiveness of the scheme is dependent on the existence of a coordinated, holistic support framework at all levels.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As a nation, giving ex-offenders second chances is not just about providing them with employment, but also believing in them and wholeheartedly accepting them as part of the community.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Notwithstanding my clarifications and suggestions, I support the Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Please allow me to address the questions and suggestions from the Members in turn.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: First, on the Employment Preparation Scheme, or EmPS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: I will first speak in Malay on family support, duration and criteria for the EmPS phases.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: (In Malay):   Mr Sharael Taha said the family plays a critical role in an inmate's rehabilitation journey.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Ms Nadia Samdin asked whether flexibility could be given to inmates lacking family support for the long home leave phase and the duration and criteria to progress through the phases for the EmPS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: I agree with Mr Sharael that strong family support can be a powerful source of motivation for an inmate to change.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The Singapore Prison Service, or SPS, recognises this.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Prior to emplacement on the EmPS, the inmate's family members will be briefed on the requirements of the scheme.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Briefings like this will allow them to better understand the scheme and encourage the inmate in his reintegration.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Inmates who progress well during the in-camp phase can transit to the home leave phases.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: This will allow them to spend more time with their loved ones and gradually reconcile with their family.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: This is because the lack of a supportive family structure may be detrimental to their reintegration.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: For these inmates, they will continue to reside at the Work Release Centre throughout the EmPS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: SPS will still allow them time-off to spend with their loved ones.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The duration an inmate spends in each phase depends on the overall emplacement period on the EmPS and SPS's assessment of whether he is suitable to progress to the next phase.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: SPS's assessment will take into account factors such as conduct and progress while on the EmPS, compliance with conditions and family support.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: SPS will also consider the inmate's attendance for work or classes, and feedback from his employers, trainers or teachers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: (In English): Mr Raj Joshua Thomas and Mr Desmond Choo asked if SPS can emplace as many eligible inmates on the EmPS as possible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Sharael Taha and Mr Yip Hon Weng asked about the eligibility for the EmPS in terms of offence committed and what can be done to mitigate the risk of re-offending.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked how the EmPS will complement the Home Detention Scheme (HDS), Conditional Remission System (CRS) and Mandatory Aftercare Scheme (MAS).

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Our intention is to emplace as many inmates as possible on community-based programmes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: As the rehabilitation of ex-offenders is one of our key missions, this is something that I can assure Members on.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: That said, we also need to put safeguards in place.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The trade-off is slightly different for each scheme, depending on their objective and scheme structure.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The Second Schedule of the Prisons Act lists the offences that will disqualify an inmate from HDS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: As the inmate will be serving his sentence in the community while on HDS, we also need to ensure public safety.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: While SPS will generally not emplace such inmates on EmPS, we need some flexibility to exercise discretion for deserving cases.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: There could be inmates who have committed such offences who could benefit from EmPS, as pointed out by Mr Raj Joshua Thomas in his speech.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Every inmate considered for EmPS will be thoroughly screened and SPS will take into consideration their response to rehabilitation and conduct in prison as part of its assessment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Only when it is assessed that they do not present a significant threat to public safety will they be considered for emplacement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: These cases will then be surfaced to an advisory committee for review and recommendation to the Commissioner of Prisons for emplacement on EmPS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Leon Perera asked if there is an appeal process.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The inmate can approach the Superintendent of the prison and approach the Board of Visiting Justices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Murali asked how the different programmes complement each other.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: There is some overlap between HDS and EmPS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Inmates on HDS will also benefit from employment, skills training or education.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The key difference is that EmPS supports inmates who require more hand-holding.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: That is why EmPS has an in-camp phase at SPS’ Work Release Centre where they can be more closely supervised and supported.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The CRS and MAS serve slightly different objectives.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: They lean more towards preventing re-offending, rather than work placement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The CRS seeks to deter inmates from re-offending when they are released on remission.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: They are subject to a basic condition that they should not be convicted of an offence committed during the remission period and be sentenced to imprisonment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Those who are at a higher risk of re-offending or need more support, will also be subjected to the MAS, a structured aftercare regime, which I mentioned in my earlier speech.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Persons on MAS may choose to work, upskill themselves or study.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: That said, all inmates will be offered assistance by YRSG, which can provide employment-related assistance to them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Together, these schemes are complementary and offer different avenues to ease inmates’ reintegration and deter re-offending.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: An inmate may be emplaced on EmPS prior to his release and, subsequently, be subject to the CRS, and even MAS, after his release.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas asked if inmates who are older or have spent a substantial period in prison could be emplaced on EmPS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: As long as inmates are eligible and found suitable, they may be emplaced on EmPS, regardless of their age or time spent in prison.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Louis Ng, Mr Desmond Choo and Mr Sharael Taha asked if the 14-day eligibility period for EmPS includes remand and at which stage inmates would be assessed for EmPS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Desmond Choo asked what tools are used to assess an inmate’s suitability.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Leon Perera asked about the process before cases are surfaced to the advisory committee.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: In practice, a person who is sentenced to imprisonment will, generally, serve more than 14 days in prison before he is emplaced on EmPS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: While in prison, he will have to undergo programmes that address his re-offending risks before he is emplaced on any community-based programme.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Towards the tail-end of the inmate’s sentence, SPS will assess the inmates’ suitability for the community-based programmes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Factors, such as progress and response to rehabilitation, conduct in prison and reintegration plan, are taken into consideration.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: During the orientation briefing for newly admitted inmates and the inmates’ regular interviews by their Personal Supervisor, the inmates will be briefed and encouraged to take ownership of their rehabilitation and maintain good conduct.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: If an inmate is not found suitable for EmPS, SPS will prepare him to be directly released at the end of his sentence and may refer him to a social service agency for assistance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng suggested that the conditions for inmates on EmPS should prohibit vice activities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: This falls under other conditions specified by the Commissioner of Prisons under the new sections 59M(1)(i) and 59M(2)(i).

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Currently, inmates emplaced on the Work Release Scheme (WRS) are already subject to this condition.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Members asked about the work, skills training and education opportunities while on EmPS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked about matching inmates with work and how skills training will be allocated to inmates.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: These are done by YRSG, which is a Statutory Board under MHA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Besides providing skills training, YRSG also provides employment-related assistance to inmates and ex-offenders.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Inmates are engaged to find out their interest in studies, work or skills training.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: As part of the employment-related assistance rendered to inmates, YRSG conducts career guidance sessions and matches inmates to jobs based on their skills qualifications and work experience.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: YRSG then engages suitable employers to interview and hire the inmates before their emplacement, or work with Continuing Education and Training (CET) Centres, to channel inmates for skills upgrading.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Ms Nadia Samdin sought clarifications on the nature of jobs offered to inmates under WRS and EmPS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Desmond Choo, Mr Sharael Taha and Mr Yip Hon Weng asked if there are plans to engage more employers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: YRSG actively engages trade associations and chambers, industry stakeholders and employers to ensure adequate job opportunities for inmates upon their release.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Employers are predominantly from the Wholesale and Retail Trade, Manufacturing, Accommodation and Food Services industries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Both WRS and EmPS will allow the inmates to take on a variety of jobs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: YRSG constantly looks out for new employers to come on board.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Melvin Yong and Mr Sharael Taha asked if EmPS could address manpower shortages in certain sectors or supply manpower to emerging sectors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Desmond Choo asked if place-and-train sectors could be developed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: YRSG pays attention to the pockets of manpower shortages which offer good career prospects.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Under YRSG’s Train and Place and Grow initiative, or TAP and Grow, YRSG partners employers, trade associations and training institutions to equip inmates with industry-specific skills.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: This facilitates the inmates’ recruitment into the relevant industries and growth in their new careers after their release.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: These initiatives help to build inmates’ skills in prison which, we hope, will translate to good employment opportunities for them after they are released.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: YRSG will continue to look out for sectors with good employment and development opportunities for inmates.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: YRSG intends to explore a similar initiative to the place-and-train scheme, where inmates will be placed on jobs upon release and undergo training during their employment to upgrade their skills.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Melvin Yong asked if the relevant authorities could review the hiring restrictions in certain sectors, such as the security sector.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: This is a balance between rehabilitation and public safety.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: For example, someone convicted of kidnapping would not be allowed to be a taxi driver.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Different occupations and sectors have their specific considerations and thus restrictions on hiring ex-offenders.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: These restrictions are deemed necessary to protect the interests of the public.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The agencies constantly review the criteria to find the most appropriate trade-off.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Nonetheless, should an ex-offender face challenges in finding employment, YRSG will assist him in finding a suitable job.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Desmond Choo, Mr Sharael Taha, Mr Yip Hon Weng and Ms Nadia Samdin asked how employers and inmates would be supported on EmPS to help inmates stay gainfully employed in the longer term.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The Jobs Growth Incentive (JGI) was introduced as an extraordinary, time-bound measure to expand local hiring amidst the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: In September 2021, the Government extended the JGI until March 2022, with stepped down support levels.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The Government will take into account the labour market’s recovery in assessing the next steps for JGI after March 2022.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: There are other ways in which we can support employers and inmates.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Inmates who are working during EmPS will be assigned a Career Coach for up to 12 months.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: This support will continue after an inmate has completed his EmPS if his emplacement period is less than 12 months.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The Career Coach provides support to help an inmate adapt to job demands and the workplace environment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The employer is also supported by the Career Coach, who helps the inmate and employer understand each other’s expectations and perspectives.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The Career Coach engages the employer and the inmate's supervisor regularly and assists to resolve any work-related issues.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: In doing so, the employer can better understand any unique need of the inmate and adopt a more effective management style.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: In partnership with the Institute for Human Resource Professionals, YRSG will be developing the coaching competencies of employers and supervisors through its Project Beyond Hiring initiative to help them develop and retain inmate or ex-offender employees better.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked if checks would be done on employers and whether there should be regulations and penalties for errant employers who exploit inmates.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Sharael Taha asked about the support available for inmates who face discrimination.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Leon Perera asked how companies will be selected and work conditions regulated to ensure fairness and worker dignity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Employers partnering YRSG are aware of inmates' needs and most of them provide on-the-job training for the inmates.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: YRSG also encourages employers keep to fair and supportive work practices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: If an inmate experiences discrimination or biased treatment at work because of his criminal records, the Career Coach will engage both the inmate and employer to resolve the issue.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: If necessary, the Career Coach may also advise the inmate to seek help from the Tripartite Alliance for Fair and Progressive Employment Practices (TAFEP).

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: More serious cases that may breach employment laws may be reported to MOM for investigation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked if inmates' salaries will be managed by SPS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: To ensure that inmates without a bank account receive their wages, YRSG works with employers to make alternative arrangements, such as issuing salaries in cash cheques in the first month of employment, to give the inmates time to open a bank account.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Desmond Choo asked if MHA could work with SkillsFuture Singapore, or SSG and e2i to upskill inmates.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Ms Nadia Samdin and Mr Sharael Taha asked about the types of training and education that inmates on the EmPS may undergo.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Leon Perera asked how training value will be ascertained.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: YRSG provides nationally accredited skills training to inmates and ex-offenders to facilitate their long-term career development and mobility.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The training is aligned to Singapore's Skills Framework developed by SSG, to ensure that inmates are trained in market-relevant skills.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: YRSG is working with SSG to explore hosting some training classes on virtual platforms as an alternative to physical lessons.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: YRSG also collaborated with e2i to host interviews between prospective employers and pre-release inmates on e2i's virtual portal.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: YRSG will also work with e2i to host workshops to equip inmates with CV-building and interview preparation skills.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Specific to the EmPS, YRSG will engage Approved Training Organisations, or ATOs and CET Centres to provide skills training for inmates on the scheme.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: YRSG is curating a set of Critical Core Skills modules for inmates on the EmPS to help them better adapt to the workplace and enhance their employability.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Formulated by SSG, the modules comprise 16 competencies that workplaces deem most essential.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: YRSG is currently exploring these modules with suitable partners and training providers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: These skills training assures employers that inmates are adequately prepared and qualified as per other workers and allows inmates to subsequently upskill as they progress in their respective careers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Other measures to ascertain training value would be through internalised and exhibited behaviour by the inmates, such as whether they successfully complete and obtain a pass grade for their training, are successfully hired by the employers and their subsequent performance on the job.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Inmates who are keen to pursue self-selected training or academic programmes after attending YRSG’s facilitated courses can do so at their own expenses, subject to SPS' approval.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Inmates on the EmPS may also pursue education such as GCE "N" to "A" levels, diploma and degree courses, if they qualify for enrolment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Sharael Taha asked if inmates can use their SkillsFuture credits.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Ms Nadia Samdin and Mr Desmond Choo asked inmates who undergo training and education will receive support such as allowances.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Leon Perera asked if inmates could benefit from subsidised rates for education fees.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: However, should an inmate wish to pursue further education after completing the YRSG-arranged courses, he will need to pay for the courses himself.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: If an inmate has financial difficulty in supporting his own training or education, he may choose to work under the EmPS, before embarking on skills training or education.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Inmates from low-income households may also apply for various Government bursaries available, such as Higher Education Community Bursary or Higher Education Bursary to subsidise their education fees.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Meanwhile, key expenses such as accommodation and training are covered during inmates’ in-camp phase, which would ease their initial finances.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Melvin Yong asked about the efforts to help inmates adapt to a society where the use of technology is increasingly prevalent.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Sharael Taha asked if inmates have access to electronic devices for training.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Leon Perera asked if ex-inmates face any impediments in accessing electronic payment services.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: SPS and YRSG have programmes in place to help inmates prepare for a digitally advanced job market and society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: In prison, inmates can use SPS-issued tablets to keep in touch with loved ones and pick up digital skills.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Since 2019, YRSG has offered the "SkillsFuture for Digital Workplace" course for inmates serving their sentence in the community.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The curriculum teaches the use of Internet banking and payments, e-communications platforms, Government e-services and basic cybersecurity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Inmates are expected to have their personal mobile devices that are required for training or learning.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: If they cannot afford one, training providers could provide loaned devices for use.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Other equipment such as laptops and computers would be provided by training providers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: If an inmate requires assistance with e-payment services, his Reintegration Officer will guide him in accessing the services.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked if inmates on the EmPS would attend classes with the public and whether identifiers associated with inmates could be removed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Inmates will attend classes with members of public and there will not be any identifiers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: For those who wear an electronic tag on the ankle, they may choose to cover it with trousers or long skirt.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: More discreet than the ankle tag, it reduces stigmatisation and boosts the inmates’ self-confidence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Ms Nadia Samdin, Mr Desmond Choo, Mr Sharael Taha and Mr Yip Hon Weng asked how co-workers and fellow classmates would accommodate the inmates and offer a conducive environment for rehabilitation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked how the needs of victims of crime can be protected from the presence of an inmate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Under the Yellow Ribbon Project, we aim to promote a more accepting society that is willing to offer ex-offenders a second chance to start afresh.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Ultimately, the safety and security of society is best served when ex-offenders successfully rehabilitate and reintegrate into society as contributing members.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We hope that employers, co-workers and classmates would give inmates and ex-offenders second chances.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Education, skills training and employment play a very important role in inmates' rehabilitation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The Government strives to strike a balance between protecting the public and providing ex-offenders the opportunity to live, work and learn in the same way as other members of society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Besides enhancing inmates' employability, it is our hope that inmates can form positive pro-social networks, assimilate into society and reduce the chances of re-offending.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We do not compel individuals to reveal their inmate or ex-offender status to avoid further stigmatisation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: If there is feedback that an inmate had misbehaved in any way towards anyone, victim or not, SPS’ Reintegration Officer will look into the matter.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: If an inmate breaches any condition or commits any offence, he may be taken off the scheme.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Melvin Yong asked about the recidivism rate of inmates on the WRS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Sharael Taha asked about the WRS emplacement figures and how abscondment would be addressed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Ms Nadia Samdin, Mr Sharael Taha and Mr Yip Hon Weng also asked if there are adequate resources catered for the EmPS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Based on SPS’ experience, the stepdown approach of the WRS has been useful and it will continue to be a feature of the EmPS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: At present, we are not expecting any significant increase in the number of inmates emplaced on the EmPS because the criteria for emplacement on the EmPS is similar to those for the WRS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: SPS has measures in place to address abscondment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: If there is any sign of possible relapse, SPS will first intensify its engagements with the inmate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The Reintegration Officer and Correctional Rehabilitation Specialist will arrange joint sessions involving the inmate, his family members and his Career Coach to address any issue.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: If an inmate absconds, SPS will work closely with the Police and CNB to re-arrest him.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: In terms of resourcing and support, SPS's Reintegration Officers and Correctional Rehabilitation Specialists are equipped with the necessary skills to supervise and support inmates in the community.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Where possible, SPS leverages technology to support its work.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: For example, SPS will be adopting biometrics to monitor inmates on the home leave phases for curfew compliance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Today, SPS verifies inmates' compliance manually via phone calls or physical checks.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: By including a fingerprint authentication function in the monitoring unit that is temporarily installed at the inmates’ home, officers can more effectively confirm that the supervisees are at home by asking the supervisees to verify their identity via the fingerprint function.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: SPS has no plans to expand the capacity at Institution S2, the Work Release Centre for the EmPS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: MHA will work within its existing resources to implement the EmPS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Leon Perera suggested that prison officers have a chance to provide pastoral care to released inmates.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: They can be posted to the Community Corrections Command as Reintegration Officers, where as a Reintegration Officer, the prison officer will supervise and guide newly released inmates who are required to comply with mandatory aftercare conditions under the Mandatory Aftercare Scheme.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Louis Ng asked for examples of minor and aggravated prison offences.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: He also asked if the Superintendent is the one who determines whether a prison offence is minor or aggravated.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: An example of a minor offence is using another inmate’s e-letter account.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: An example of an aggravated offence is open defiance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The Superintendent follows sections 72 and 73 in determining if a prison offence is minor or aggravated and may punish the inmate accordingly if the inmate is found guilty of the offence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: There are checks and balances in place to ensure that inmates are dealt with appropriately for committing prison offences.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: For instance, under section 71, if a Superintendent imposes punishment on an inmate who had committed an aggravated offence, the Superintendent is required to notify the Commissioner.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The Commissioner may then confirm or vary the punishment imposed by the Superintendent.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: If the Commissioner does not agree with the punishment, she may direct a re-investigation into the case.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: There have been instances where an aggravated prison offence was reduced to a minor prison offence, after re-investigation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Louis Ng sought clarifications on the prison offences that would be applicable to inmates on the EmPS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: If an inmate commits a prison offence such as quarrelling with or assaulting another inmate at his workplace, it will not be considered as “within prison”.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Clause 24 of the Bill is clear on this.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Such acts would be classified as breaches of the conditions of his EmPS order under section 72(1)(48).

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: SPS will investigate and take appropriate disciplinary action against inmates who have committed such breaches.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: If an inmate commits an aggravated assault outside prison, the case will be reported to the Police for criminal investigations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: SPS does not take disciplinary action against inmates who commit self-harm outside prison.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Instead, SPS will provide the necessary assistance and interventions to address the supervisee’s self-harm tendencies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked how many inmates have had their release deferred in order to carry out any outstanding Court-ordered punishment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: As mentioned in my speech earlier, on average, there were nine inmates per year whose release was deferred by the Commissioner under section 50I(3) of the Prisons Act and four inmates per year whose detention was extended by the Court under section 326 of the Criminal Procedure Code (CPC), in order to carry out outstanding Court-ordered punishment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Murali Pillai gave a scenario where the Commissioner of Prisons could be placed in a conflicted position.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: And like what I explained earlier, there should not be a situation where the Commissioner is put in a conflicted position.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng suggested that instead of increasing the period of deferment under section 50I(3) of the Prisons Act, we could review the 14-day period for filing a Notice of Appeal.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: In the event that an appeal is filed, whether within the 14-day period or by invoking section 380(1) of the CPC, SPS will seek the Court’s direction on whether to release the inmate or to detain the inmate under section 326 of the CPC.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Both powers under section 50I(3) of the Prisons Act and section 326 of the CPC, serve to ensure justice takes its course.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Ms Nadia Samdin asked if the processing time of correspondence between inmates and their families would be affected.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We do not foresee any changes to the processing time needed for written correspondence between inmates and their loved ones as the screening process will not be affected.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Leon Perera asked about the checks and balances in place for the new regulations on inmates’ correspondence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: As I mentioned in my opening speech, correspondences will only be withheld when they undermine the security or good order of the prison or incite the commission of any offence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Prison officers are mindful of the sensitivities involved in processing and screening inmates’ correspondence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: While every attempt is made to preserve the confidentiality of inmates’ letters, any content with security implications will be surfaced for consideration by a superior officer, to decide if the letter should be withheld.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: He also asked how the prescribed persons would know if the information crosses the threshold.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: MHA is still reviewing the type of information that breaches the threshold.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: However, I had provided some clear examples in my speech earlier.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: On another part, I would just like to share that the Prisons Act does not prescribe any punishment for breaching these provisions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We would also like to clarify that these amendments are not an attempt to stop inmates' communication and prevent them from speaking out about genuine grievances or give feedback.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Based on the example provided by the hon Member, where an inmate communicates about his injuries suffered in prison, we will not withhold or redact such correspondence, unless it is assessed to affect the security or good order of the prison or incite the commission of an offence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Therefore, the context of the communication is important to the facts of the case.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: So, when the correspondence written by an inmate is withheld, he will be informed and he will be given a letter-form to re-write his letter if he chooses to do so.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: An inmate will also be informed if any correspondence addressed to him is withheld.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: The inmate may ask his personal supervisor as to why the letter was withheld and the reason will be shared with the inmate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Leon Perera also asked if SPS could provide financial literacy courses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: This is already being done as part of the pre-release programme.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: SPS also works with community partners to run enrichment programmes for inmates on the EmPS, including financial literacy programmes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: He also asked about if SPS could partner other banks, besides POSB, to set up bank accounts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We assessed that currently, this is sufficient, as POSB is commonly used.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Having said that, we will monitor the demand and situation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: He also asked about the allowances and the salaries the inmates get.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: I would like clarify that there is a difference between work programmes in prison and work in the community.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: For work programmes in prison, they are given allowances.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: If they work in the community, YRSG will match the inmates to jobs that offer market-rate salaries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: He also asked one question that I have covered in my Malay speech, whereby he asked what about those inmates without family support.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: As I said in my Malay speech, inmates without strong family support may still be emplaced on the EmPS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: However, they may not progress to the home leave phase.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: So, for these inmates, they can continue to reside at the Work Release Centre throughout EmPS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: So, we will do our best to give the opportunity to all eligible inmates because we believe that as part of the rehabilitation and reintegration process, the support from the family, community and employment is very important.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: I met many people who really have given very good support to what we are doing with regard to the EmPS and they realise that this will help to enhance the skills and the opportunities of the inmates.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Mr Murali Pillai went a step further to suggest that talented ex-offenders be given a chance to perform at NDP 2022 and we thank him for his suggestion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: We will continue to galvanise the community and employers to act together for second chances.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Through community-based programmes such as the EmPS, we hope that inmates have the opportunity to boost their work experience, improve their education, or deepen their skillsets.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim
text: Eventually, these will help them to create long-term career development and mobility, allowing them to show that they are contributing individuals at work and to an accepting society.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: I was going to say that I thought that the Minister of State was very thorough, and we did not need clarification, but I see a hand.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I agree the Minister of State was very thorough and I do not intend to take up more of the House's time.
